citation.title: De-homogenization using Convolutional Neural Networks
citation.authors: Martin O. Elingaard, Niels Aage, J. Andreas Bærentzen, Ole Sigmund
citation.venue: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: The generated designs have compliance-volume performance 7–25% worse than the homogenization solution while requiring only a fraction of the computational cost.
claim.key_phrase: at a fraction of the computational cost
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Conclusion states a factor 5 to 10 faster than existing de-homogenization; 5 is the lower stated factor, not a measured same-hardware ratio. Section 4.2.1 estimates the range from a cited 10 s least-squares step on different hardware.
claim.alternatives: Section 4.2.1 estimates 5–10× faster de-homogenization than Groen et al.; the same section extrapolates roughly 10,000× versus full fine-mesh top88 TO; conclusion repeats 5–10×.

baseline.classical_method: Homogenization-based TO with classical least-squares de-homogenization [16]; top88 fine-mesh density TO also compared (Section 4.2.1)
baseline.implementation: Cited Groen et al. de-homogenization and MATLAB top88 (Section 4.2.1)
baseline.hardware_classical: Modern laptop for cited Groen et al. timing; top88 hardware not stated (Section 4.2.1)
baseline.hardware_ml: Single Intel Core i7 2.6 GHz CPU for tables; NVIDIA Titan X GPU for training (Section 4.1)
baseline.problem_size: 60×30 coarse to 1440×720 or 2400×1200 fine elements (Tables 2, Section 4.2.1); 240×120 to 5760×2880 (Table 3)
baseline.classical_iterations: About 1000 fine-mesh top88 iterations estimated; coarse homogenization solved until convergence, count not stated (Sections 4, 4.2.1)
baseline.classical_time: About 10 s for cited 80×40 to 1600×800 least-squares stage; top88 about 16 s or 87 s per iteration at 1440×720 or 2400×1200 (Section 4.2.1)
baseline.training_time: At most 1 hour for 15 epochs on NVIDIA Titan X GPU (Section 4.1)
baseline.data_generation_cost: 20,000 synthetic orientation fields; generation time not stated (Sections 3, 4.1)
baseline.quality_metric: FE compliance multiplied by realized volume fraction, normalized to homogenized reference; both reported separately (Table 2 caption, Section 4.2)
baseline.quality_gap: 7–25% worse compliance-volume performance claimed in abstract; Section 4.2 reports 25.7% and 22.3% mean gaps for two wavelengths, and 13% for high-resolution inputs; returned volumes overshoot reference by 5.7% or 2.4% on average (Section 4.2, Tables 2–3)

R1.evidence: Abstract and Section 4.2: speed advantage is asserted alongside 7–25% worse physical performance; no equal-quality or equal-time comparison. Section 4.2.1 also omits the coarse homogenization solve from de-homogenization timing.

R2.evidence: Section 4.2.1: fine-mesh comparator is MATLAB top88 and cited least-squares timing comes from different hardware; efficiency relative to a strong baseline is not directly established.

R3.evidence: Sections 3 and 4.1: synthetic training set of 20,000 fields and training of at most 1 hour are reported, but data-generation time and amortized break-even uses are absent; Section 4.2.1 limits its direct 5–10× estimate to de-homogenization.

R4.evidence: Tables 2–5 and Section 4.2: FE compliance and realized volume are given for final designs, including volume overshoot; no infeasible/disconnected design rate is reported.

reporting.n_test_cases: 3 problem classes (Michell, double-clamped, L-shaped; Section 4), with multiple parameter configurations (Tables 2–5)

notes: The 5–10× comparison uses a cited de-homogenization time from a different laptop; the four-orders-of-magnitude top88 comparison extrapolates 1000 iterations and excludes the coarse TO solve.
